newsitem.title: USA: IBM chief sees many opportunities for growth.
newsitem.headline: IBM chief sees many opportunities for growth.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. Chairman Louis Gerstner said Wednesday that IBM has many opportunities for growth -- but reiterated the computer giant's goal is for revenues to rise in the high single digits, unlike some high-tech companies.

"We have enormous opportunities within IBM," Gerstner said in his fourth annual meeting with Wall Street analysts. But because of IBM's size, the $76 billion colossus will not grow at the explosive rates of some meteor-like technology firms.
"Our model is to procure high single-digit revenue growth," he told analysts.
"We are not going to be like most information technology companies," Gerstner said. "We are not going to grow 40 to 50 percent a year. That's hard to do."
He said he called fast-growing tech companies "meteors" because some eventually burn up.
"We are focused on growing shareholder value," Gerstner said. "We have a model that is not the model of the meteors."

In its most recent first-quarter earnings report, IBM had revenue growth of 9 percent, on a constant currency basis. The company had stellar growth in its services business, which grew 28 percent, amid a drop in some hardware revenues, such as mainframe computers, minicomputers and workstations.
Analysts asked Gerstner if he ever expects to see IBM's System 390 mainframes, once the company's biggest revenue and profit generator, grow again.

Gerstner said that in the past three years IBM has slashed prices of mainframes by 80 percent, which has helped fuel stronger demand. And with more and more computers linked on corporate networks accessing the massive amounts of data stored in these machines, demand for these big data repositories grows. But Gerstner declined to predict growth.
"I'm not going to count on the 390 becoming a great growth engine again, as much as Linda (Sanford, general manager of IBM's System 390 business) will tell me, 'Just watch,'" Gerstner said.
Instead, Gerstner pointed to software and services as the company's growth engines.

He added that software has not yet performed as well as its services business because the company clung to IBM software that runs on its mainframe systems instead of developing software distributed over computer networks.

"We are the Rodney Dangerfield of the software industry," Gerstner joked, referring to the comedian whose mantra was he did not get any respect. "And to a certain extent, we deserve it. We gave software away on our hardware, we watched software go distributed and we hung onto our host stuff."
Total software sales fell 2.9 percent in the first quarter.
The decline was mostly attributable to mainframe software.
Gerstner said a new growth area for IBM is in distributed and so-called "middleware" software, which connects its host mainframe software to other diverse computers.
IBM's purchases of Tivoli Systems and of Lotus Development Corp. were strategic investments in this area, Gerstner said.
He also told analysts that IBM's hard disk drive business had such high double-digit growth that it was almost at three digits. In addition, personal computers have made a huge comeback.
"Four years ago, Compaq (Computer Corp.) was kicking sand in our face," Gerstner said. In the first quarter, IBM's PC unit growth and PC revenue growth outpaced Compaq's, the PC industry leader.
Gerstner also highlighted some IBM achievements, such as making it possible for American Airlines customers to make reservations and buy tickets over the Internet.
